notes.meaning: Once the judge Ehud passed away, the people of Israel turned away from God again. During their long years of peace, they grew careless and fell back into worshiping idols. Without a faithful leader to guide them, their old sinful habits quickly returned.

Because Israel disobeyed, the Lord allowed a powerful Canaanite king named Jabin to conquer them. To be sold into an enemy's hand means God handed them over as discipline for their sins. Jabin ruled from the northern stronghold of Hazor, and his general Sisera commanded a feared army.

The Canaanite army had nine hundred iron chariots, giving them a terrifying advantage over Israel's foot soldiers. Jabin treated the people cruelly for twenty long years. In their deep misery, the Israelites finally turned back to the Lord and begged Him for help.

During this dark period, God raised up Deborah to lead the nation. A prophetess was a woman who received messages directly from God to share with the people. She served both as a spiritual guide and as a judge who settled disputes across Israel.

Deborah held court out in the open, sitting under a well-known palm tree in the hill country of Ephraim. People traveled from all over the land to bring their disagreements and legal cases to her. Her open-air seat showed that she was fair, accessible, and widely respected.

Deborah sent for a warrior named Barak and delivered God's clear instructions to him. He was ordered to gather ten thousand men from the northern tribes of Naphtali and Zebulun and march to Mount Tabor. This battle plan was not Deborah's idea, but a direct command from the Lord.

The Lord promised that He would draw General Sisera and his chariots out to the Kishon River. Even though the Canaanite chariots seemed unbeatable, God assured Barak that Sisera's forces would be delivered into his hands. God was setting a trap that the enemy general could not see.

Barak agreed to fight only if Deborah came with him to the battlefield. He knew her presence would assure the soldiers that God was with them and keep their courage high. While he showed genuine faith in God's message, his demand also showed that he leaned heavily on the prophetess.

Deborah agreed to go with him, but she warned Barak that he would not win personal honor from this campaign. Because he hesitated, the Lord would hand Sisera over to a woman instead of a mighty warrior. Deborah then traveled north with Barak to begin assembling the army.

Barak called together ten thousand volunteer fighters from the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali. These men marched out as simple foot soldiers without any cavalry or war chariots. Deborah accompanied them up to Mount Tabor to strengthen their confidence in God.

A man named Heber had separated from his fellow Kenites and set up his tent far north near Kedesh. The Kenites were relatives of Moses' family who usually lived in the southern desert. This note is placed here to explain how Heber's family was living right where the coming drama would unfold.

Word soon reached Sisera that Barak had led an army to the top of Mount Tabor. Mount Tabor was a high, steep hill that protected the Israelite infantry from chariot attacks. Hearing that the Israelites were gathering for war prompted Sisera to respond immediately.

Sisera assembled all nine hundred of his iron chariots and his whole army at the Kishon River. The flat valley seemed like the perfect ground for his wheeled chariots to run over the Israelite foot soldiers. Sisera felt confident of an easy victory, unaware that God was drawing him into danger.

Deborah told Barak to move immediately because the Lord had already handed Sisera over to him. She reminded him that God Himself was marching out before their army to fight for them. Trusting this word, Barak and his ten thousand men gave up their high safety on the mountain and charged down into the open valley.

The Lord threw Sisera, his charioteers, and his entire army into wild panic and confusion. The chariots became useless in the chaotic rush of the battle. Realizing that his army was completely broken, Sisera abandoned his royal chariot and ran away on foot.

Barak chased the fleeing chariots and troops all the way back to their home base. Sisera's powerful army was completely wiped out by the sword during the retreat. Not a single Canaanite soldier was left alive on the battlefield.

While his army fell, Sisera escaped on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite. He fled there because King Jabin had a peaceful treaty with Heber's household. Sisera believed he would find safety among people who were on good terms with his king.

Jael came out of her tent to greet the tired commander and invited him inside, telling him not to fear. She gave him a place to lie down and covered him with a rug or blanket. Her warm hospitality made the exhausted general feel completely secure.

Sisera asked Jael for a little water because he was thirsty from the heat and his long run. Instead of plain water, she opened a skin of curdled milk and gave him a rich drink. After he drank, she covered him up again, which helped him drift quickly into a heavy sleep.

Sisera ordered Jael to stand guard at the tent opening. He told her to lie and say that no one was inside if any pursuers came searching for him. He trusted that ancient rules of tent privacy would keep anyone from looking past her.

While Sisera slept deeply from exhaustion, Jael picked up a wooden tent pin and a mallet. As a nomad woman, pitching tents was part of her daily work, so she handled the tools with skill and strength. She crept quietly to his side and drove the peg through his temple into the ground, killing him on the spot.

When Barak arrived hot on Sisera's trail, Jael came out and offered to show him the man he was hunting. Barak followed her inside and found his enemy lying dead with the tent peg driven through his head. Just as Deborah had foretold, the glory of defeating the opposing general went to a woman.

The scripture reminds us that God Himself subdued King Jabin before the Israelites that day. The defeat of Sisera's army broke the backbone of Canaanite power in the north. This miracle showed Israel that their true rescuer was the Lord alone.

After this great victory, Israel kept pressing their advantage against King Jabin. Their power grew steadily until they completely broke his kingdom and destroyed him. God turned twenty years of harsh oppression into total freedom for His people.
